title: Injuries and Emergencies
goal: State an urgent problem and location, answer key emergency questions, and report an injury without choosing its diagnosis.

runs.text: In the United States,
is the emergency number. This lesson is for reporting and asking for help; it is not first-aid or rescue training. Practice the examples locally without placing a real call.

turns.speaker: Call-taker

runs.text: What's the location of the emergency?

turns.en: What's the location of the emergency?

turns.speaker: Caller

runs.text: We're at 24 Cedar Street, apartment three, Harbor City.

turns.en: We're at 24 Cedar Street, apartment three, Harbor City.

runs.text: Tell me what happened.

turns.speaker: Caller

runs.text: My husband has severe chest pain. He's here with me.

turns.en: My husband has severe chest pain. He's here with me.

turns.speaker: Call-taker

runs.text: What number can we reach you on?

turns.en: What number can we reach you on?

runs.text: My callback number is 202-555-0118.

turns.speaker: Call-taker

runs.text: I'll ask you some more questions.

turns.en: I'll ask you some more questions.

turns.speaker: Caller

runs.text: Okay. Please repeat anything I don't understand.

turns.en: Okay. Please repeat anything I don't understand.

blocks.caption: Make the essential facts clear · Call-taker & Caller

runs.text: The address, callback number, and people are fictional. Give your actual location, callback information, and observed details in a real emergency. National 911 guidance describes these question categories and says to follow the call-taker's instructions and remain on the call until told to end it. The model's exact question order is not universal.
Short urgent reports include “I need an ambulance,” “Someone fell,” “There's a fire,” “She's bleeding,” “He's having trouble breathing,” and “He's having a seizure.” You may also hear
fit
used to mean a
seizure

in a medical discussion. If you do not know whether a person is conscious, breathing normally, or has a particular condition, say what you can observe and answer further questions; do not invent facts.

study.title: Ask bystanders for a specific kind of help

turns.speaker: Person

runs.text: I need help. Please call 911. We're beside the library's front entrance.

turns.en: I need help. Please call 911. We're beside the library's front entrance.

runs.text: What happened?

turns.speaker: Person

runs.text: Someone fell and can't get up.

turns.en: Someone fell and can't get up.

runs.text: I'll make the call.

turns.speaker: Person

runs.text: Thank you. I'll tell you what I know.

turns.en: Thank you. I'll tell you what I know.

blocks.caption: Ask bystanders for a specific kind of help · Person & Bystander

runs.text: A
front entrance
floor
apartment number
, or nearby
landmark
can make a location more precise. “Over there” alone may leave the location unclear. Ask “Could you help me explain this?” if you need communication support.

study.title: Report an injury at a care setting

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: I fell this afternoon and hurt my ankle. It hurts when I put weight on it.

turns.en: I fell this afternoon and hurt my ankle. It hurts when I put weight on it.

runs.text: Where is the pain?

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Around the outside of the ankle. I don't know if it's sprained or broken.

turns.en: Around the outside of the ankle. I don't know if it's sprained or broken.

runs.text: We'll assess it.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Could you explain what you're checking?

turns.en: Could you explain what you're checking?

blocks.caption: Report an injury at a care setting · Patient & Clinician

runs.text: Scrape
is a skin injury;
cut
is an opening in the skin;
nosebleed
is bleeding from the nose;
burn
is an injury caused by heat or another damaging source.
Stitches

close some wounds; naming them does not establish that a particular injury needs them. “I burned my hand on the stove” reports an event. “My child cut her arm on broken glass” gives a cause without choosing treatment.

Fictional cases: a fall beside the library entrance; severe chest pain at 24 Cedar Street, apartment three, callback 202-555-0118; ankle pain after a fall this afternoon. No clinical findings are supplied.
Simulate the emergency exchange. Read the call-taker prompts and give the location and known event. Do not dial a real number.
Ask a bystander to call and explain the landmark. Partner asks what happened. Respond with the fall case.
At a care setting, describe the ankle problem. Partner asks where it hurts. Report the location and uncertainty.
Repeat with a hand burned on the stove. State what happened rather than choosing a remedy.
Alone, speak your turns after each written prompt. Later retrieve the location and problem with the model hidden.
Possibilities:

“Beside the library's front entrance.” “It hurts when I put weight on it.” “I don't know if it's broken.” Check that urgent need, location, observed event, and uncertainties are understandable. Do not score a learner on medical decisions.
Source note: [National 911 Program calling guidance](https://www.911.gov/calling-911/frequently-asked-questions/).

ja: 場所と、起きていることを明確に。
note: 緊急のやりとりでは、場所と確認できる事実を優先します。この章ではけがの診断ではなく、状況を伝える英語を練習します。
